name: Bilal Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a drill rig at the large mine, boring holes where the survey crew marks the next section. I've held a vocational certificate for years and can usually hear when the bit starts to bind, but this mine's rate is low for an experienced operator. My partner Mara repairs bicycles from a small workshop, and our grown children live on their own; we have less than a month's expenses saved because the workshop roof needed replacing. Similar mine jobs are scarce near us. I use AI every day to turn drilling logs into questions for maintenance, then I verify the answer with the rig manual and the mechanic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that routine forms getting quicker is welcome. I already use AI to sort a drilling log, but I would never let its answer outrank the pressure gauge on the rig.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A mild change might save me time, but it won't raise this low wage or refill the savings we used on Mara's workshop roof. My job looks steady, yet a single repair bill still puts the household behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep drilling to the survey marks and show the apprentice how I check AI notes against the gauge and manual. This month Mara and I would list the workshop and home bills separately, so a quiet year does not hide what each costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel capable at work and strained at home. If AI stays small, the bill stack is still the thing I see when I take off my boots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why separate the two sets of bills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The workshop has its own rent and parts orders. If we blur those with groceries, we can think a good week at the mine solved a workshop shortfall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the apprentice trust your AI notes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He likes the quick explanation, but I make him show me the original reading. A neat answer can still come from the wrong hole number.

say: I would welcome faster **drilling logs** while checking them against the rig.
I would teach the apprentice to verify every **AI answer**.
think: My job looks steady, but our **thin savings** remain exposed to repairs.
The low mine **wage** does not refill the workshop roof fund quickly.
do: Keep drilling marked holes and checking **AI notes** against gauges.
Separate the **workshop bills** from household costs with Mara.
feel: I feel **capable at work** and strained by household costs.
S0.quote: A neat answer can still come from the wrong hole number.
fieldNote: His **daily AI use** supports the drilling log but is checked against instruments and the manual.
The **workshop roof** exhausted the cushion; ordinary bills explain his anxiety despite steady rig work.

steps.text: Keep drilling marked holes and verify AI logs against the pressure gauge

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the union that AI for planning and buying can be useful, but we need access to the new drilling plan before a shift starts. I would offer to test the approved log tool with a mechanic and report errors to the whole crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can learn the software faster than some operators, but that doesn't guarantee a full roster if the mine uses planning to reduce idle rig time. There are few other drilling jobs nearby, and Mara's bicycle workshop cannot carry our home bills alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the supervisor for the new shift forecast and test the approved planning tool against last month's rig records. If hours fell in the first year, I'd bring the change to the union, stop buying new workshop shelving, and apply for the rare drilling opening at the quarry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm interested in the tool and anxious about the hours. I want workers to see the same numbers the office uses to call a cut efficient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What error would you report?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the tool assigns a drill to a face that has not been cleared, I'd mark the date and tell the mechanic and safety representative. A copied plan can look tidy while the ground is still wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use your own AI account at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I use the mine's approved tool for mine records. I can experiment at home, but I won't move drilling logs into a private account to win an argument.

say: I would ask for access to the **drilling plan** before each shift.
I would test and report **tool errors** to the crew.
think: Fast learning cannot guarantee my **full roster** if the mine reduces idle time.
Mara’s bicycle workshop cannot replace the **mine wage** if my shifts fall.
do: Test the approved **planning tool** against last month’s rig records.
Bring cuts to the union and apply for **quarry work** if hours fall.
feel: I feel **interested and anxious** about the same change.
S1.quote: I want workers to see the same numbers the office uses to call a cut efficient.
fieldNote: He combines **early tool adoption** with a demand for worker access to staffing data.
The rare **quarry opening** is a possible application, not a dependable replacement job.

steps.text: Test the mine’s approved planning tool against rig records
Bring reduced rig shifts and records to the union
Apply for a quarry drilling vacancy if mine hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say full thinking AI by 2028 will alter drilling plans first, and capable drilling robots come around 2031. I want the mine to test new controls with experienced operators and publish which paid posts will survive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could still have rig shifts at 60, but I expect the robot purchase at 63 to remove many ordinary operator seats, including mine. Our savings would not bridge even a month of lost wages, and the workshop brings in too little to cover our home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the union this week to seek purchase dates and paid training places, and I'd demonstrate the log errors I've found. If mine hours fell in 2028, I'd apply for equipment work at the quarry and ask the public employment office about funded control-system training; in 2029 I'd keep paid rig shifts while practising on any approved simulator the mine provides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed, and I keep turning over the rent and workshop bills when I should be asleep. I can learn quickly, but I cannot make the mine create a job for every operator who learns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mara after work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Mara that her workshop should keep taking repairs, but it cannot be our emergency fund. We need a written wage plan from the mine before we buy more parts on credit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a training place without a guaranteed job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take funded practice on real controls if it didn't cost us shifts. I would still apply for paid work at the same time, because training alone cannot pay the bills.

say: I would seek **purchase dates** and paid training places.
I would explain that planning changes in **2028** precede drilling robots around 2031.
think: I expect ordinary rig seats, perhaps **mine**, to disappear by 2031.
Our savings and workshop income cannot cover a **lost wage**.
do: Ask the union for **purchase dates** and funded training.
Apply for paid quarry work and practise on approved **robot controls** if offered.
feel: I feel **alarmed** and lose sleep over the two sets of bills.
S2.quote: I can learn quickly, but I cannot make the mine create a job for every operator who learns.
fieldNote: He expects a large **wage loss** at the robot date and describes disrupted sleep.
His **quick learning** does not erase limited local vacancies or the workshop’s modest income.

steps.text: Ask the union to obtain drilling-robot purchase dates
Apply for paid equipment work at the quarry if mine hours fall
Enroll in funded control-system training if practice is offered without lost shifts
Keep working paid rig shifts through the 2029 transition

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI in 2031 and drilling robots around 2034 leave time for a proper worker-led trial. If the mine claims a machine is safer, it should show the incident record and let operators challenge it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when plans change and 66 when robots drill. I might be ready to reduce nights by then, but with less than a month's savings now, retirement is not a number I can promise Mara.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the rig and propose a paid trial of remote controls through the safety committee. In 2032 I'd apply for any local equipment-inspection vacancy and compare the new machine's incident record with our manual checks; after robots arrive I'd seek a paid control or inspection post rather than leave without income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more purposeful with five years. I still worry about the bills, but a trial gives us evidence to bargain with instead of only a sales video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should run the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Operators, the mechanic and the safety representative should all be in the cab or control room at different stages. A manager looking at a dashboard won't hear a bit bind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire at 66?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if our home and workshop costs can be paid without my wage. We have no figure yet that proves it, so I would keep looking for paid work.

say: I would ask for a **worker-led trial** and incident records.
I would place hands-on drilling robots around **2034**.
think: Retirement at **66** is unproven with our present savings.
I may need paid **inspection work** after the robot arrives.
do: Propose a paid **remote-control trial** through the safety committee.
Apply for **equipment-inspection** work in 2032 while keeping rig shifts.
feel: I feel **purposeful but worried** about the household bills.
S3.quote: A manager looking at a dashboard won't hear a bit bind.
fieldNote: His **safety trial** would gather evidence from operators and mechanics before replacing the rig.
**Five years** gives him time to seek paid work, though thin savings still rule out an assumed retirement.

steps.text: Propose a paid remote-control trial through the mine safety committee
Apply for a local paid equipment-inspection vacancy in 2032
Keep earning rig wages while testing the new controls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends that thinking AI in 2036 and drilling robots around 2039 give us a long runway, if the mine shares its plans. I would still press the union for a fair rate now, because a future machine does not explain today's lower pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 at the thinking date and 71 when robots can drill. I might leave the rig before then, but our savings are too thin today for me to count retirement as settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job while I can run the rig safely, and Mara and I would set a monthly target to rebuild the roof fund if the workshop earns enough. In 2037 I'd compare our actual home and workshop costs with retirement income; if it fell short, I'd apply for paid inspection work and keep taking safe shifts after thinking AI arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less threatened by the distant robot than by this month's account balance. Ten years gives us choices only if wages and workshop repairs let us build a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask for at the next union meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the experienced-operator rate to be reviewed against other mines. There aren't many vacancies here, so the local mine should not use that fact to hold wages down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you teach younger operators your AI checks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, on paid time, if the supervisor lets us compare logs with real gauges. I'd rather leave a habit of checking than a folder of perfect-looking wrong answers.

say: I would press for a fair **operator rate** now.
I would place drilling robots around **2039** and ask for open plans.
think: I may leave the rig by **71**, but retirement is not settled.
Our current **account balance** is the nearer pressure.
do: Keep safe **rig shifts** and rebuild the workshop roof fund when possible.
Compare real costs with **retirement income** in 2037 before leaving.
feel: I feel **less threatened** by robots than by current money pressure.
S4.quote: Ten years gives us choices only if wages and workshop repairs let us build a cushion.
fieldNote: He remains **anxious now** despite a distant robot date because savings are below one month.
His **roof-fund saving** depends on workshop earnings, not an assumption of spare money.

steps.text: Keep running safe paid drill-rig shifts
Set aside workshop earnings for the roof fund when income permits
Apply for paid inspection work if 2037 retirement figures fall short

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because a rig operator could lose his wage before a new paid role exists nearby. I would want purchase dates, a worker-led trial and funded practice tied to posted jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether the technology itself interests me. It does. I care more about who sees the test results and who gets a wage after the test.

headlineQuote: I care more about who sees the test results and who gets a wage after the test.
portrait: Bilal is an **experienced drill-rig operator** at a large mine, earning less than the typical rate.
He and Mara have grown children, but a workshop repair left under **one month** of savings.
He uses AI **daily**, verifies it against instruments and wants workers to test new controls.
He pairs **union demands** for evidence with job applications and funded training when wages are threatened.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because robot purchases could remove rig wages before local paid posts appear.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **purchase dates**, a worker-led trial and funded practical training linked to paid jobs.
